title: The zoning envelope: what you may build before anyone says yes
summary: Every site comes with an invisible box of rights: height, floor area, setbacks, coverage, parking and use. This lesson teaches how to read that box, how to tell an as-of-right building from one that needs permission, and the ladder of approvals you climb when you want more than the box allows.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the zoning envelope is the building the law already allows on a site, and everything you want beyond it must be asked for, granted, and paid for. Know the envelope before you price the land, because the gap between the envelope and your plan is where entitlement risk lives.

Recall

Q. In land diligence, what does a reliance letter give you?

A. The right to rely on a consultant's report that was prepared for someone else. Without it, the consultant's duty usually runs only to the client who engaged them, so a wrong report may leave you with no claim.

Q. What is an easement?

A. A right held by someone else to use your land for a defined purpose, such as a utility line or a right of way. It runs with the land, so it binds you as the next owner.

Q. What separates tax avoidance from tax evasion?

A. Avoidance arranges affairs within the law, though anti-avoidance rules can still deny a benefit; evasion hides or misstates facts and is a crime. Where the line sits in a given system must be verified against the primary source.

Why this matters

Land is priced on what can be built on it. If you assume a building the rules do not allow, you will overpay, and the overpayment is not a rounding error: land sits at the bottom of the development stack, so a small change in the permitted building moves the land value hard. When you run your own projects, nobody hands you the envelope. You must read it from the plan, the by-law and the title, and you must know the difference between what is yours today and what you are hoping to be given.

The envelope: six dimensions of a box you cannot see

Plain English first. Picture a transparent box sitting on the lot. Zoning draws its walls and its lid. Your building has to fit inside it. Most zoning codes define the box with six things.

  1. Use. What activities are permitted: residential, commercial, hotel, mixed.
  2. Density. How much floor area or how many units the lot may carry. Many codes use a floor area ratio, which means the total building floor area divided by the lot area.
  3. Height. A maximum in metres or storeys, sometimes with angular planes that step the building back as it rises.
  4. Setbacks. Minimum distances from the front, side and rear lot lines.
  5. Coverage. The share of the lot the building footprint may occupy.
  6. Parking and loading. Minimum stalls per unit or per area, which often bind before anything else does.

The professional framing: the envelope is the zoning envelope, the maximum built form permitted on a site under current rules. A building that fits it entirely is as-of-right, meaning it needs only a building permit and standard technical review, not a discretionary decision by a council or board. That distinction matters more than any other in this lesson. As-of-right is a right; anything beyond it is a request.

Worked example one: which limit binds

Hypothetical round numbers. A lot of 2,000 square metres. Floor area ratio 2.0, so the density limit allows 4,000 square metres of floor area. Height limit four storeys. Coverage 50 percent, so the footprint may be 1,000 square metres. Setbacks of 6 metres front and rear and 3 metres each side on a lot 40 metres wide by 50 metres deep leave a buildable area of 34 by 38 metres, which is 1,292 square metres, so coverage at 1,000 is the tighter of the two.

Now stack it. A 1,000 square metre footprint over four storeys gives 4,000 square metres, which happens to equal the density limit. So far the box allows about 4,000 square metres, or roughly 45 units at a hypothetical 88 square metres gross each.

Then parking. Suppose the code demands 1.25 stalls per unit and surface stalls need about 30 square metres each including aisles. Forty-five units need 56 stalls and 1,680 square metres of surface. With a 1,000 square metre footprint, the lot has only 1,000 square metres left, and setbacks eat part of that. Parking binds. Either you go underground at real cost, or you cut units until the stalls fit. The lesson: compute every limit, and the smallest one is your building. The parking ratio here is invented for teaching; read the actual by-law.

Say that out loud now.

Compute every limit. The smallest one is my building. Everything beyond it is a request, not a right.

The entitlement ladder

An entitlement is a legal permission to develop land in a particular way. When your plan sits outside the envelope, you climb a ladder, and each rung costs more time and carries more risk than the one below.

  • Pre-application consultation. An informal meeting with planning staff before you file. It costs little and tells you what they will support, oppose, or ask for.
  • Minor variance or site plan approval. Small relief from a numeric standard, such as a setback reduced by one metre, usually decided by a committee or board against stated tests.
  • Rezoning or plan amendment. A change to the rules for the site itself, decided by the elected council after public notice and a hearing. This is the big rung.
  • Conditions. Approvals almost always arrive with conditions: road widening, a park contribution, infrastructure upgrades, design changes, fees.
  • Appeal. Either side, and sometimes neighbours, may challenge a decision before a tribunal or court, depending on the system.
  • Development agreement. A contract between the developer and the authority setting out obligations in exchange for the approval, often registered on title so it binds later owners.

Worked example two, hypothetical. You want 60 units instead of the 45 the box allows. That needs a rezoning. Planning staff at pre-application say they would support 55 with underground parking, a 3 metre road dedication, and a contribution to a local park. Your 15 extra units are now 10 extra units, with conditions attached, and a council vote, a notice period and a possible appeal sit between you and a building permit. Each rung must be priced in time and money, which Sage does on Day 3.

How the best do it

Large institutional developers generally write an entitlement strategy before they close on land: the as-of-right building, the target building, the rungs needed to get there, the decision-makers at each rung, the likely conditions, and the timeline with a downside case. They do not leave approvals to the architect alone. What a small developer can copy costs almost nothing: a one-page entitlement strategy in the site file, signed off by a planner, before any money goes unconditional.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing the land on the target building instead of the as-of-right building. If the approval fails, shrinks or arrives three years late, you have paid for density you do not own. The control: value the land at the as-of-right envelope, and pay for the difference only through a condition in the purchase contract, a price that steps up on approval, or an option. Day 2 shows what happens without that control.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the height and density limits and stopping. The beginner sees "four storeys, ratio 2.0" and multiplies. The professional reads the parking schedule, the setbacks, the angular planes, the title for registered agreements, and the official plan, and only then knows the box. Professional sign-off required: a registered planner, to confirm the envelope before you rely on it.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: an approval can raise value before a single wall goes up, and how that uplift is taxed on a sale depends on the system; verify against the primary source. Liability: a development agreement registered on title binds you and every future owner to its obligations. Banking: lenders lend on approved density, not hoped-for density. Governance: record who decided to pursue each rung and on what evidence. Estate: unentitled land held for years can be hard to value in an estate. Exit: a buyer pays for granted, unappealable approvals, and discounts everything else.

Callback

In Week 31 you learned the four tests of highest and best use, starting with what is legally permissible. This lesson is that first test opened up. Legally permissible means the envelope today, plus whatever you can realistically win, priced as risk rather than assumed as fact.

Recap

The envelope is the building the rules already allow: use, density, height, setbacks, coverage and parking, and the smallest limit wins. As-of-right is yours; everything above it is climbed rung by rung and comes with conditions. Price land on the box, and buy the upside only with contractual protection. Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics, a rezoning that was paid for before it was granted.
checklist: Read the zoning by-law, the official plan and the title before pricing any site
Compute density, height, setbacks, coverage and parking separately
Name the binding limit and build the as-of-right scheme from it
List every approval rung the target scheme needs
Hold a pre-application meeting before filing anything
Value the land on the as-of-right envelope, not the target building
Write a one-page entitlement strategy with a downside timeline
Have a registered planner confirm the envelope in writing
head: Field checklist
speak: The zoning envelope is the building the rules already allow on a site. It has six dimensions: use, density, height, setbacks, coverage and parking. You compute each limit separately, and the smallest one is your building. Parking often binds first. A building that fits the box is as-of-right: you need a building permit, not a political decision. Anything bigger is a request, and you climb a ladder to get it: a pre-application meeting, then a minor variance or a rezoning, then conditions, a possible appeal, and often a development agreement registered on title. Every rung costs time and money and can shrink what you get. So price the land on the as-of-right building, and buy the upside only through a purchase condition, a price that steps up on approval, or an option. Write a one-page entitlement strategy before you go unconditional, and get a planner to confirm the envelope.
terms: Zoning envelope — the maximum building form a site's current zoning permits, defined by use, density, height, setbacks, coverage and parking.
As-of-right — development that complies fully with current zoning and needs only a building permit, not a discretionary approval.
Development agreement — a contract between a developer and an authority setting the developer's obligations in exchange for an approval, often registered on title.

hostile.q: Your land price assumes 60 units and the site is zoned for 45. Why should I lend against 60?
hostile.a: You should not, and I am not asking you to. The land is priced on the 45-unit as-of-right scheme. The extra density is bought only if the rezoning is granted and free of appeal, through a price step-up in the purchase agreement. Until then the loan and the equity are sized on 45, and the entitlement strategy, with its downside timeline, is in the file.

role: Failure forensics (with Cole, audit and integrity)
title: The rezoning that was paid for before it was granted: a composite
summary: A developer paid a price for land that only made sense if a rezoning was approved, closed unconditionally, and then watched the approval shrink, attract heavy conditions and stall on appeal. This composite case walks the seven steps of failure and ends with the rule that keeps entitlement upside from being paid for in advance.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the most expensive words in land are "the rezoning is a formality." This case shows how a developer paid in cash today for a permission that was never his, and how every stage after closing made the gap wider.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between an as-of-right building and one that needs a discretionary approval?

A. As-of-right fits the current zoning and needs only a building permit. A discretionary approval, such as a rezoning, depends on a decision by a council or board that may say no, say less, or attach conditions.

Q. Why does a quitclaim or a plain transfer protect a buyer less than title insurance?

A. A transfer only passes whatever the seller had. Title insurance pays for covered defects in that title, up to the policy limit, even if the seller could not have known about them.

Q. What does an engagement letter with a professional adviser need to state?

A. The scope of the work, who the client is, what the adviser is relying on, the fees, and any limits on liability. A vague scope is how advice misses the real risk.

Why this matters

Entitlement failures rarely look like disasters on the day. Nothing collapses. A meeting goes badly, a condition arrives, a neighbour files an appeal, a year passes. The damage is in the carrying cost, the lost density and the price already paid. Because no single public case teaches this cleanly enough to name, Cole and I have built one from patterns that recur. This is a composite example. The names and numbers are invented; the sequence is real.

The case in seven steps

Step 1, timeline. Month 0: a developer agrees to buy a 2,000 square metre lot zoned for about 45 units. The seller asks a price that only works at 70 units. Month 2: the developer waives the purchase conditions to beat another buyer and closes. Month 5: he files a rezoning for 70 units. Month 11: planning staff recommend 55, with underground parking, a road widening and a park contribution. Month 14: council approves 55. Month 15: a residents' group appeals. Month 31: the appeal is settled at 52 units with added design conditions. Month 36: the building permit issues. The pro forma had assumed permits at month 12.

Step 2, key decisions. Three decisions carried the outcome. Agreeing a price set by the target density. Waiving the conditions before filing anything. And filing for the maximum rather than for what pre-application advice suggested staff would support.

Step 3, assumptions. That a nearby site rezoned two years earlier was a reliable precedent. That the council would weigh housing need over neighbour objection. That appeals were rare. That conditions would cost about the same as on the precedent site. Each was a guess dressed as a fact.

Step 4, incentives. The seller was paid on closing and carried none of the approval risk. The broker was paid on closing. The architect was paid to design the largest building. The developer's lender on the land had lent against an appraisal that used the target density. Nobody in the chain was paid to say "price it at 45."

Step 5, warning signs ignored. The pre-application meeting, held after closing, produced a written note that staff "may support moderate intensification" with "significant infrastructure contributions." The neighbourhood had an active residents' association. The precedent site had a different road frontage and an existing sewer upgrade. All of this was on file and none of it changed the plan.

Step 6, point of no return. Waiving the conditions. Before that, the developer could have walked, renegotiated, or made part of the price contingent on approval. After it, the seller had the money and the developer had a permission he did not yet own.

Step 7, root cause. Paying a certain price for an uncertain right. The entitlement risk was transferred entirely to the buyer, at the seller's valuation, without any contractual mechanism to share it.

Say that out loud now.

A certain price for an uncertain right is a bet the buyer has already lost half of.

Worked example one: what the gap cost

Hypothetical round numbers. The price paid was 3.5 million dollars, which the seller justified at 50,000 dollars per approved unit on 70 units. At 45 as-of-right units the same per-unit rate supports 2.25 million. At the 52 units finally approved it supports 2.6 million. So the developer overpaid by about 900,000 dollars against the outcome, before counting anything else.

Now add time. Permits arrived 24 months later than planned. Carrying 3.5 million of land at a hypothetical 9 percent cost of money is about 315,000 dollars a year, so roughly 630,000 dollars of extra carry. Add appeal legal and consultant costs, say 200,000 dollars, and conditions costing 400,000 dollars more than the precedent. The total damage against the plan is above 2 million dollars on a 3.5 million dollar land purchase. The numbers are invented; the structure of the loss is not.

Worked example two: the contract that would have shared the risk

Same deal, different paper. Base price 2.25 million dollars, payable on closing, which is the as-of-right value. A step-up of 50,000 dollars per unit approved above 45, payable only when the rezoning is final and the appeal period has expired, capped at 70 units. At 52 approved units the step-up is 7 units times 50,000, which is 350,000 dollars, for a total of 2.6 million. The seller still shares the upside; the buyer pays for density only once it exists. The 24 months of carry are now on 2.25 million, not 3.5 million, saving about 225,000 dollars a year at the same hypothetical rate.

Cole's audit note

Cole reads an entitlement file looking for three documents. A written as-of-right valuation dated before the price was agreed. A pre-application record dated before the conditions were waived. And a schedule tying each part of the price to an approval event. If any of the three is missing or dated after the money moved, the risk was never priced, only hoped for. Cole would also ask who wrote the appraisal and on what density instruction, because an appraisal instructed to assume the target is not evidence of anything.

Reading it from the seller's side

It helps to understand why the seller pushed so hard. A landowner who has watched a neighbour rezone believes the uplift belongs to the land, and in a sense it does: the approval will attach to the site, not to the applicant. What the seller is really doing is asking to be paid for the uplift without carrying the risk of getting it. That is a reasonable thing for a seller to want and an unreasonable thing for a buyer to give. Once you see it that way, the negotiation is no longer about the number. It is about who carries the risk between today and the final approval, and a step-up is simply the honest answer to that question.

The biggest risk

Mistaking a precedent for a promise. Another site's approval tells you what one council decided about one site at one time. The control is to treat every approval as a probability with a timeline, priced in the contract, and to get the pre-application advice in writing before any money goes unconditional.

The beginner's mistake

Filing for the maximum to "leave room to negotiate down." Councils and neighbours often hear the maximum as the developer's real intent, and the fight that follows costs time that a realistic first filing would have saved. File for what you can defend.

Callback

In Week 16, Sage taught that a valuation must distinguish as-is from as-complete value, and that value depending on future approvals is a hope until it is granted. This case is that lesson with real money attached: the appraisal valued the hope, and the price followed it.

Recap

The developer agreed a price set by target density, waived conditions before testing the planners' view, filed for the maximum, and absorbed shrinking density, heavy conditions and a two-year appeal. The root cause was paying a certain price for an uncertain right. Rule 32 below is the control. Next: Sage on The Money, how to put a value on entitlement risk and the time it takes.
checklist: Value the site at as-of-right density before agreeing any price
Hold the pre-application meeting before conditions are waived
Tie any price above as-of-right value to a final, unappealable approval
Treat precedents as evidence of probability, never as promises
File for the density you can defend, not the maximum
Budget carry for a downside approval timeline
Check what density the appraiser was instructed to assume
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 32: I pay today only for the zoning a site has today; any price for density not yet granted is paid only when the approval is final and free of appeal.
speak: This is a composite case. A developer agreed a land price that only worked at 70 units on a site zoned for 45. He waived his conditions to beat another buyer, then filed for the maximum. Staff recommended 55 with heavy conditions, council approved 55, neighbours appealed, and the settlement came in at 52, two years late. Against the outcome he overpaid by about 900,000 dollars and carried the land for two extra years. The point of no return was waiving the conditions before the planners' view was in writing. The root cause was paying a certain price for an uncertain right. The fix is in the contract: pay the as-of-right value on closing, and pay a step-up per extra unit only when the approval is final and the appeal period has run. Rule 32: I pay today only for the zoning a site has today.
terms: Entitlement risk — the chance that an approval is refused, reduced, delayed or burdened with costly conditions.
Price step-up — a contract term that increases the purchase price when a defined event, such as a final approval, occurs.
Appeal period — the window after a decision during which it can be challenged, before the approval is final.

hostile.q: The seller will not accept a step-up. Another buyer will pay the full price unconditionally. Why not match it?
hostile.a: Because the full price buys a permission the seller does not have. If another buyer wants to carry that risk at the seller's valuation, I let them. I will offer the as-of-right price unconditionally, or a higher total with the step-up. If neither works, I walk, and I keep my capital for a site where I am paying for what exists.

title: Pricing a permission: probability, time and the cost of conditions
summary: An entitlement is worth what it adds to land value, multiplied by the chance of getting it, minus the cost of the conditions, minus the cost of waiting. This lesson turns that sentence into a calculation you can defend to a lender, and closes with what entitlement risk means for a personal balance sheet.
body:
Mr Shabazz, an approval you do not yet hold is worth its uplift, discounted for the chance it fails, the conditions it brings and the time it takes. Put those three on paper and you will stop paying for hope.

Recall

Q. When a broker presses you to waive diligence conditions early, what is your position?

A. No condition is waived until every diligence stream is complete, in writing and priced. A deadline set by the other side is not evidence about the land.

Q. How can an unregistered or unresolved title issue reduce what a lender will advance?

A. The lender's security depends on clean title. An encumbrance it cannot rank ahead of, or a defect not covered by title insurance, leads to a lower loan, a holdback, or a condition that must be cleared before funding.

Q. Why do tax penalties matter to a project's returns even if the tax is eventually paid?

A. Penalties and interest are pure leakage: they add cost with no asset behind them, and a dispute ties up time and cash. Verify any penalty regime against the primary source.

Why this matters

Entitlement is where the largest value is created in development, often before construction starts. It is also where the largest sums are lost by people who treat a probable outcome as a certain one. If you can price a permission honestly, you can negotiate land with confidence, size your own risk capital, and explain to a lender why you are or are not paying for density. If you cannot, the seller, the broker and your own optimism will do it for you.

The four parts of an entitlement's value

Plain English first. Ask four questions. How much more is the land worth if I win? How likely am I to win? What will winning cost me in conditions and fees? How long will it take, and what does waiting cost?

The professional framing: risk-adjusted entitlement value equals the land value uplift, multiplied by the probability of approval, minus the expected cost of conditions and the pursuit, minus the carrying cost of time. The uplift is the difference between the residual land value at the target density and at the as-of-right density. The probability is a judgement, not a fact, so you document how you reached it: pre-application advice, the plan's policies, comparable decisions, and the strength of local opposition.

Worked example one: the expected value of a rezoning

Hypothetical round numbers, carried forward from earlier in the week. As-of-right, 45 units, residual land value 2.25 million dollars. Target, 55 units after staff advice, residual land value 2.75 million before conditions. Uplift: 500,000 dollars.

  1. Probability. Pre-application support from staff, a plan policy favouring intensification, and moderate neighbour opposition. You judge 65 percent. Expected uplift: 0.65 times 500,000 is 325,000 dollars.
  2. Conditions. A road widening, a park contribution and upgraded underground parking, estimated at 180,000 dollars, payable only if approved. Expected cost: 0.65 times 180,000 is 117,000 dollars.
  3. Pursuit costs. Planner, architect, traffic study and legal fees of 150,000 dollars, spent whether you win or lose.
  4. Time. Eighteen months at a hypothetical 9 percent cost of money on the 2.25 million dollar land value is about 304,000 dollars of carry, which you would bear partly even on the as-of-right path. Suppose the as-of-right scheme could have started in six months; the extra twelve months cost about 203,000 dollars.

Add it up: 325,000, minus 117,000, minus 150,000, minus 203,000, equals a negative 145,000 dollars. On these numbers the rezoning destroys value. That is a real answer, and a common one for small uplifts.

Say that out loud now.

Uplift times probability, minus conditions, minus pursuit, minus time. If the answer is negative, build what the box allows.

Worked example two: when the rezoning pays

Change one input. The target is 70 units, staff support it, and the uplift is 1.25 million dollars. Probability 60 percent gives 750,000. Conditions of 300,000 at 60 percent cost 180,000. Pursuit 200,000. Extra time 12 months, about 203,000. The result is roughly positive 167,000 dollars. Now the rezoning is worth pursuing, but only just, and only if you have not already paid the seller for it. If you paid 1.25 million for the uplift on closing, your expected result is the 167,000 minus the 1.25 million you handed over, a loss of about 1.08 million. That is Rule 32 in numbers.

What it does to the returns

Time attacks the internal rate of return, which measures return per unit of time, more than it attacks profit. An extra year of approvals on a three-year project can cut the levered internal rate of return sharply even if the final profit barely moves, because the equity is tied up longer. Lenders feel it as well: a land loan that was meant to be refinanced at permit now needs an extension, usually at a fee, and the debt service coverage ratio, which compares income to debt payments, is irrelevant because there is no income at all. Land carry is paid entirely from equity or interest reserve. So the entitlement timeline is a funding question as much as a value question.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On a personal balance sheet, money spent pursuing an approval is the riskiest asset you own. It produces no income, it is illiquid, and it can go to zero. Warrick's rule is to treat pursuit costs as risk capital: sized so that losing all of it would not touch your liquidity floor, the cash reserve you keep for living and emergencies. A developer who funds an appeal with money he needed for next year has turned a planning risk into a personal one. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal allocation.

Turning the number into a negotiation

The calculation is not only for you. It is the most useful thing you can put in front of a seller who believes the uplift is already his. Show him the four lines. Most landowners have never seen the cost of conditions or the carry written down, and when they do, a step-up price stops looking like a trick and starts looking like arithmetic.

Hypothetical. The seller wants 3.5 million dollars for the 70-unit case, which is the as-of-right value plus the whole 1.25 million uplift. You offer 2.25 million on closing plus a step-up of 50 percent of the realised uplift when the approval is final. If the 70 units are granted, he receives about 2.88 million in total; if 52 are granted, he receives less; if the application fails, he keeps 2.25 million and his land is no worse off than today. He shares upside he could not have captured alone, and you pay for density only when it exists. Your lender sees a land loan sized on the as-of-right value, which is the only value it would have lent on anyway. The share of uplift you offer is commercial practice, not a standard; it moves with the market and the seller's alternatives.

The biggest risk

Choosing the probability to make the answer positive. The control is to write the probability, with its reasons, before running the numbers, and to have someone who is not paid on the outcome, often your planner, give their own figure. If yours is much higher, explain the gap or use theirs.

The beginner's mistake

Forgetting that pursuit costs are spent win or lose, and that conditions are spent only if you win. Mixing the two overstates the downside of trying and understates the cost of succeeding. Keep them in separate lines.

Callback

In Week 15 you learned that the internal rate of return rewards speed and can make a slow, profitable project look poor. Entitlement time is the clearest case: the profit can survive a delay that the internal rate of return does not, which is why you report both, and why a lender asks about the timeline before the margin.

Recap

Price an approval as uplift times probability, minus conditions, minus pursuit, minus time. Small uplifts often fail the test; large ones can pass, but only if you have not already paid the seller for them. Treat pursuit money as risk capital on your own balance sheet. Next: REGA on The Rules, how planning law decides what a council may ask for and how an appeal really works.
checklist: Calculate the uplift as target residual minus as-of-right residual
Write the approval probability and its reasons before running the numbers
Ask your planner for an independent probability
Keep pursuit costs and condition costs in separate lines
Price the carry for a downside approval timeline
Report profit and internal rate of return side by side
Size pursuit money as risk capital above your liquidity floor
head: Field checklist
speak: An approval you do not hold has four parts to its value. The uplift: how much more the land is worth at the target density than as-of-right. The probability of getting it, written down with reasons. The cost of conditions, which you pay only if you win. The pursuit costs and the carry, which you pay win or lose. Multiply the uplift by the probability, subtract the expected conditions, subtract pursuit, subtract time. On a small uplift the answer is often negative, and the right move is to build what the box allows. On a large uplift it can be positive, but only if you have not already paid the seller for it. Time hurts the internal rate of return more than profit, and land carry comes entirely from equity. On your own balance sheet, pursuit money is risk capital: size it so losing all of it leaves your liquidity floor intact.
terms: Risk-adjusted entitlement value — the uplift from an approval times its probability, less expected conditions, pursuit costs and carrying cost.
Pursuit costs — the fees and studies spent seeking an approval, incurred whether or not it is granted.
Carry — the cost of holding land over time, chiefly interest or the opportunity cost of equity, plus taxes and insurance.

hostile.q: Your 65 percent approval probability looks invented. How do I know you did not pick it to make the deal work?
hostile.a: Because it was written before the model, with its reasons: written staff advice, the plan policy and three comparable decisions. My planner, who is not paid on the outcome, gave 55 percent. At 55 the rezoning is still negative, which is why the plan is to build the as-of-right scheme and treat the rezoning as optional.

title: The rules of permission: plans, by-laws, conditions, variances and appeals
summary: Planning law separates the policy that guides a decision from the rules that bind it, and it limits what an authority may demand in return for an approval. This lesson explains how those limits work in concept, how variances and appeals are decided, and why a development agreement is a contract you must read as one.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a planning approval is a public decision made under rules, and those rules cut both ways: they limit what you may build, and they limit what the authority may ask of you. Knowing both halves is what lets you negotiate conditions instead of simply accepting them.

Recall

Q. What are the three commercial outcomes of an adverse diligence finding?

A. Reprice, hold back money in a reserve, or walk. Saying nothing means you absorb the cost.

Q. What does it mean that a registered interest "runs with the land"?

A. It binds whoever owns the land, not only the person who agreed to it, so a buyer inherits it on purchase.

Q. What is the idea behind a general anti-avoidance rule?

A. It lets a tax authority deny a benefit from an arrangement that complies with the letter of the law but abuses its purpose. The exact test and its limits vary by system; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

You will spend more time with planning authorities than with any other government body. If you treat every request as a demand you cannot question, you will accept conditions that cost more than they should and approvals that take longer than they must. If you treat the authority as an opponent, you will lose its goodwill, which is worth more than any argument. The professional path is in between: know the legal frame, and use it to have better conversations, not to pick fights.

Policy, rules and decisions

Plain English first. There are two layers of planning documents. The first is policy: a long-range plan that says what the community wants the area to become. It goes by different names, such as official plan, comprehensive plan or master plan. The second is rules: the zoning by-law or ordinance that turns policy into numbers for each site. A rezoning changes the rules for your site, and it generally has to be consistent with the policy above it.

The professional framing: decisions come in two broad kinds. Some are legislative, such as a council changing the zoning, where elected members have wide discretion and the public is entitled to notice and to be heard. Others are closer to adjudication, such as a committee deciding a variance against fixed tests, where the decision-maker must apply those tests and give reasons. The kind of decision changes how much discretion exists and how it can be challenged. Which category a given approval falls into depends on the system; verify against the primary source.

Applied example, hypothetical. Your site's zoning allows four storeys, and the plan above it designates the corridor for "mid-rise intensification up to eight storeys." That policy does not give you eight storeys. It means a rezoning request for five storeys starts from a position the plan supports, which raises your probability on Day 3's calculation and shapes how you frame the application.

What an authority may ask for

Conditions are the price of an approval. They are lawful, common and often reasonable: a road widening so traffic can move, a contribution to parks, a sewer upgrade, a design change. But in most mature systems an authority cannot demand anything it likes. The broad principle is that a condition must serve a genuine planning purpose connected to the development, and its burden must bear some relationship to the development's impact.

In the United States that principle has a constitutional form. Two Supreme Court cases, Nollan v. California Coastal Commission in 1987 and Dolan v. City of Tigard in 1994, are widely taught for the ideas of an "essential nexus" between a condition and the project's impact, and "rough proportionality" between the two. Other systems reach similar ideas through statute or administrative law. Treat this as the concept only, and verify how it applies where you build against the primary source.

Worked example one, hypothetical. Your 55-unit approval comes with three conditions: a 3 metre road dedication along your frontage, a park contribution of 120,000 dollars, and the reconstruction of an intersection two blocks away at 600,000 dollars. The first two are typical and plainly connected to your project. The third may be a cost the authority wants a developer to absorb for a wider problem. You do not refuse it in the meeting. You ask, in writing, for the traffic study that links your project's trips to that intersection, and for the share of trips your project generates. If your project causes 10 percent of the intersection's added traffic, a proportionate share might be 60,000 dollars, not 600,000. Professional sign-off required: a land-use lawyer and a transportation engineer, before you argue it.

Say that out loud now.

Conditions are lawful and normal. They must connect to my project and bear some proportion to its impact. I ask for the link in writing.

Variances and appeals

A variance is permission to depart from a numeric standard without changing the zoning, such as reducing a side setback from 3 metres to 2.4 metres. Systems apply tests that sound different and aim at the same thing: is the relief genuinely small, does it respect the intent of the plan and the rules, and is it appropriate for the site? Some systems frame it as a hardship test. The exact test must be verified against the primary source for the jurisdiction.

An appeal is a challenge to a decision before a tribunal, board or court. Three questions decide whether one matters to you. Who has standing, meaning who is allowed to appeal: only the applicant, or neighbours and community groups as well? What is the deadline? And does the appeal body hear the matter fresh, or only review whether the original decision was lawful? A system where neighbours can appeal and the tribunal hears everything again carries far more timeline risk than one where only the applicant can appeal and review is narrow. Never assume the deadline or the standing rules; verify them against the primary source.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Council approves your rezoning in month 14. The appeal window, under the invented rules of this example, is 20 days and neighbours have standing. Your lender's commitment requires a final, unappealable approval. So the earliest date you can treat as final is the day after the window closes with no appeal filed, and your land purchase step-up should be tied to that date, not to the council vote. One sentence in the contract saves you from paying for an approval that a neighbour then unpicks.

Development agreements

A development agreement is a contract with the authority, and you read it the way LEX taught you to read any contract: obligations, timing, security, default and remedies. It often requires security, such as a letter of credit, for works you must build, and it is often registered on title so it binds the next owner. Check what triggers release of the security, what happens if your project is delayed or abandoned, and whether the obligations survive a sale of part of the site.

The biggest risk

Treating the council vote as the finish line. An approval is not final until appeal rights have expired, and conditions are not complete until the development agreement is signed and its security posted. The control is an approvals register with each item's status: granted, final, conditions met, agreement signed, security released.

The beginner's mistake

Trying to influence decision-makers privately. Many systems restrict contact with members during a hearing process, require lobbyists to register, or treat gifts to officials as an offence. Speak to staff through proper channels, and to elected members only in the ways the rules permit. Verify the rules where you build.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught that a letter of intent can bind in some clauses and not others, and that the label does not decide it. A development agreement is the opposite case: it is plainly binding, it often outlives your ownership, and it is drafted by the stronger party. Read it as hard as you would read your own lender's commitment.

Recap

Policy guides, rules bind, and decisions can be legislative or closer to adjudication. Conditions are normal but must connect to your project and bear some proportion to it. Variances answer small departures; rezonings answer big ones; appeals turn on standing, deadline and scope. A development agreement is a contract that may run with the land. Next: Sage on The Numbers, working backward from an approved building to what the rezoning was worth.
checklist: Read the policy plan above the zoning before framing any request
Identify whether each approval is legislative or closer to adjudication
Ask in writing for the study linking each condition to your project
Estimate your project's proportionate share of any off-site works
Confirm appeal standing, deadline and scope against the primary source
Tie payments and closings to final, unappealable approval dates
Read the development agreement for security, default and survival on sale
Contact decision-makers only through permitted channels
head: Field checklist
speak: Planning law has two layers. Policy says what the community wants an area to become; the zoning rules turn that into numbers for each site. A rezoning changes the rules for your site and must generally fit the policy. Decisions can be legislative, with wide discretion, or closer to adjudication, with fixed tests and reasons. Conditions are the normal price of approval, but in most mature systems they must connect to your project and bear some proportion to its impact. In the United States that idea is taught through the Nollan and Dolan cases. So when an off-site condition looks large, ask in writing for the study that links it to your project. A variance handles a small departure. An appeal turns on who has standing, the deadline and whether the matter is reheard. An approval is final only when appeal rights expire. A development agreement is a contract that often runs with the land, so read it like one.
terms: Official plan — the long-range policy document that guides land use, which zoning rules must generally be consistent with.
Variance — permission to depart from a specific numeric zoning standard without changing the zoning itself.
Standing — the legal right to bring an appeal or challenge a decision.

hostile.q: The intersection works are a condition of approval. If you push back, staff will recommend refusal. Why risk the whole approval over 600,000 dollars?
hostile.a: I am not refusing the condition. I am asking, in writing and politely, for the traffic study that links our project to that intersection and for our share of the added trips. If the study supports the full amount, we pay it and it goes in the pro forma. If it shows a smaller share, we propose a proportionate contribution. That is a normal conversation, and it keeps the relationship intact.

title: Reverse engineering a rezoning: how many extra units must it win to pay?
summary: Start from a finished, approved building and work backward to the land value each extra unit creates, then to the smallest rezoning that covers its own costs and the most you could rationally pay for a site today. Every step uses hypothetical round numbers with units shown.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a rezoning is only worth chasing if the extra units it wins pay for the conditions, the fees and the time. Today we start from the finished building and work backward to that break-even number, and then to the highest price you should pay for the land.

Recall

Q. In the zoning envelope, which limit decides the building?

A. Whichever is smallest once density, height, setbacks, coverage and parking are each computed. On many small sites the parking requirement binds first.

Q. Why does an easement for a buried utility line often reduce what you can build?

A. Because you usually cannot build over it or excavate near it without the holder's consent, so it removes part of the lot from the buildable area and may constrain foundations.

Q. Why should a tax saving in a pro forma carry a confidence label?

A. Because a saving that depends on an interpretation an authority may reject is a contingent benefit, not a certain one. Show it separately and verify the position against the primary source.

Why this matters

Most people run a rezoning forward: here is the extra density, here is the extra profit, let us apply. Working backward is more honest. You fix the result you need and ask what must be true to get there. That reveals the small rezonings that can never pay, at any probability, before you spend a dollar on consultants. It also gives you a number to say to a seller who wants paying for an approval nobody has yet granted.

Step 1: from the finished building to land value per unit

Start with the outcome. A completed, approved building where each unit sells for 400,000 dollars, all figures hypothetical.

  1. Sale value per unit: 400,000 dollars.
  2. Required developer profit at 15 percent of value: 0.15 times 400,000 equals 60,000 dollars per unit. This margin is commercial practice, not a standard.
  3. Development cost per unit excluding land, covering hard, soft and finance costs and contingency: 290,000 dollars.
  4. Residual land value per unit: 400,000 minus 60,000 minus 290,000 equals 50,000 dollars.

So each approved unit is worth 50,000 dollars of land value. At the 45-unit as-of-right envelope, the land is worth 45 times 50,000, which is 2.25 million dollars. This is the same figure the week has used, now with its derivation shown. In real projects the cost per unit rises when density forces underground parking, so the per-unit residual falls for the extra units; we hold it flat here to keep the arithmetic visible.

Step 2: the fixed costs of trying

Now list what a rezoning costs regardless of how many units it wins.

  • Pursuit costs: planner, architect, studies and legal, 150,000 dollars, spent win or lose.
  • Extra carry: twelve more months of holding 2.25 million dollars at a hypothetical 9 percent cost of money, which is 202,500 dollars. Round to 203,000.
  • Conditions if approved: road widening, park contribution and parking upgrade, 180,000 dollars, paid only if the approval is granted.
  • Probability of approval: 65 percent, written down with reasons before the calculation.

Step 3: solve for the break-even number of extra units

Call the number of extra units x. The expected gain is the probability times what you win if approved, minus what you spend either way. Set it to zero.

0.65 times the quantity 50,000 x minus 180,000, minus 150,000, minus 203,000, equals zero.

  1. Move the fixed costs across: 0.65 times the quantity 50,000 x minus 180,000 equals 353,000.
  2. Divide by 0.65: 50,000 x minus 180,000 equals about 543,000.
  3. Add 180,000: 50,000 x equals about 723,000.
  4. Divide by 50,000: x equals about 14.5.

So the rezoning needs to win at least 15 extra units, taking the building from 45 to 60, before it pays for itself on these assumptions. The 55-unit scheme that staff supported in this week's example wins 10. It fails.

Say that out loud now.

Fix the result, then solve for what must be true. If the break-even is above what the planners will support, do not apply.

Step 4: could any probability rescue ten extra units?

Work it backward again. Hold the extra units at 10 and solve for the probability that would make the expected gain zero.

  1. If approved, 10 units win 10 times 50,000, which is 500,000 dollars, minus 180,000 of conditions, leaving 320,000.
  2. Fixed costs are 353,000 dollars.
  3. Required probability: 353,000 divided by 320,000 equals about 1.10, or 110 percent.

A probability above 100 percent is impossible. Even a certain approval at 10 extra units loses about 33,000 dollars. That is the value of working backward: one line of division retires an idea that would otherwise have consumed a year and 150,000 dollars of fees.

Step 5: the most you should pay for the land today

Now the larger case. Staff support 70 units, which is 25 extra. The approval would win 25 times 50,000, or 1.25 million dollars, before conditions of 300,000, leaving 950,000. Pursuit costs rise to 200,000 dollars for the bigger application and the extra carry stays at 203,000. Probability 60 percent.

  1. Expected net win: 0.60 times 950,000 equals 570,000 dollars.
  2. Subtract fixed costs: 570,000 minus 200,000 minus 203,000 equals 167,000 dollars.
  3. Maximum land price paid wholly on closing: as-of-right value 2.25 million plus the expected value of the rezoning, 167,000, equals about 2.42 million dollars.

The seller who asks 3.5 million on the strength of 70 units is asking you to pay 1.08 million dollars more than the rational all-cash price. Anything above about 2.42 million should only be paid as a step-up when the approval is final, which is Rule 32 expressed as a ceiling. Professional sign-off required: a registered planner on the probability and a cost consultant on the condition estimates, before this ceiling becomes an offer.

Step 6: test the generous assumption

Step 1 held land value at 50,000 dollars for every unit. Suppose the extra units force a small underground garage and the land value of each extra unit falls to 35,000 dollars. Rerun Step 3.

  1. 0.65 times the quantity 35,000 x minus 180,000 equals 353,000.
  2. Divide by 0.65: 35,000 x minus 180,000 equals about 543,000.
  3. Add 180,000 and divide by 35,000: x equals about 20.7.

The break-even rises from 15 extra units to 21, taking the building from 45 to 66 units. A modest change in the cost of the extra units moved the break-even by six units. That is why the per-unit figure must be rebuilt, not reused.

The biggest risk

Holding the per-unit residual flat when it is not. Extra units often trigger a parking garage, a second stair or a heavier structure, which raises the cost per unit and shrinks the 50,000 dollars. The control is to rebuild the per-unit residual for the target scheme with its own cost estimate, not to reuse the as-of-right figure.

The beginner's mistake

Running only the forward case. The forward case always produces a number, and a number feels like permission. The backward case tells you whether the number is even reachable. Run both, and if they disagree, believe the one that asks what must be true.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught you to reverse engineer a deal from public information: implied land price, rent and return. This lesson applies the same move to a permission. Instead of asking what a buyer must have believed to pay a price, you ask what an approval must deliver to justify its cost.

Recap

Derive the land value each approved unit creates, list the fixed costs of trying, and solve for the break-even number of extra units and the break-even probability. Small rezonings often cannot pay at any probability. The rational all-cash land price is the as-of-right value plus the rezoning's expected value, and anything above it is paid only on a final approval. Next: Pax in The Room, a pre-application meeting and a community meeting.
checklist: Derive residual land value per unit from sale value, profit and cost
List pursuit costs, carry and conditions separately
Write the probability and its reasons before solving
Solve for the break-even number of extra units
Solve for the break-even probability at the supported density
Rebuild the per-unit residual for the target scheme's real costs
Cap the all-cash land price at as-of-right value plus expected value
Have a planner and a cost consultant confirm the inputs
head: Field checklist
speak: Work a rezoning backward. Start from the finished building: 400,000 dollars a unit, minus 60,000 of required profit, minus 290,000 of cost, leaves 50,000 dollars of land value per approved unit. Then list the costs of trying: 150,000 of pursuit, about 203,000 of extra carry, and 180,000 of conditions if approved, with a 65 percent chance. Solve for the extra units that make the expected gain zero. The answer is about 15. The scheme staff support wins 10, so it fails. Hold it at 10 and solve for the probability that would rescue it, and you get 110 percent, which is impossible. For a bigger 70-unit case, the expected value is about 167,000 dollars, so the most you should pay all in cash is about 2.42 million. Anything above that is paid only as a step-up when the approval is final.
terms: Break-even density — the smallest number of extra approved units at which a rezoning's expected gain covers its costs.
Break-even probability — the approval probability at which a rezoning's expected gain is exactly zero.
Residual land value per unit — the land value each approved unit supports, after sale value less cost and required profit.

hostile.q: Your break-even assumes 50,000 dollars of land value for every extra unit. The extra units need a parking garage. Isn't your number too generous?
hostile.a: Yes, it is the generous case, and I said so. With a garage the cost per extra unit rises and the land value per extra unit falls, which raises the break-even above 15 units. Since the generous case already fails at 10 extra units, the conclusion holds: we build the as-of-right scheme. If we pursue the 70-unit case, the per-unit figure will be rebuilt from a garage estimate first.

title: The pre-application meeting and the community hall
summary: Two rooms decide most entitlements: the planner's meeting table and the community hall. This lesson scripts both, with the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind each question, when to stay silent, and how to stay steady when a room turns against you.
body:
Mr Shabazz, in the planner's office your job is to learn what they will support before you commit to anything; in the community hall your job is to be believed. Neither room is won by winning arguments.

Recall

Q. In this week's composite case, what was the point of no return?

A. Waiving the purchase conditions before the planners' view was known and in writing. After that, the buyer carried all the entitlement risk at the seller's price.

Q. When a title search reveals an encroachment, what are your first two moves?

A. Get the surveyor to confirm and measure it, and have your lawyer advise whether it can be resolved by agreement, by a registered easement, or must be priced or walked away from.

Q. If an adviser suggests an arrangement that sounds too good, what question do you ask?

A. What is the commercial purpose apart from the tax result, and would the arrangement survive the anti-avoidance rule? Then verify the answer against the primary source.

Why this matters

Planners and residents are not obstacles; they are the people whose judgement your land value depends on. A planner who trusts you will tell you early what will fail. A community that believes you will argue less, appeal less, and sometimes support you. Both are built or lost in the first meeting, and both are lost faster than they are built. You will be in these rooms long before you have a building to show.

Room one: the pre-application meeting

The scene. A small meeting room. A senior planner, a junior planner taking notes, and a transportation engineer from the authority. You, your planner and your architect. You have a site plan, a massing sketch and one page of numbers. You have not yet waived your purchase conditions, which is the whole point of being here now.

Lines to say:

  • "Thank you for the time. We want to hear your concerns before we design further, not after."
  • "The site is zoned for about 45 units. We are exploring up to 55 because the corridor policy supports mid-rise. What would make that supportable, and what would make it hard?"
  • "Which studies would you expect to see with an application, and at what level of detail?"
  • "Are there conditions you would typically ask for on a site like this?"
  • "Could we confirm the main points in a short note after today?"

Lines never to say:

  • "The site next door got eight storeys, so we expect the same." It sounds like entitlement, and the planner knows the differences you do not.
  • "We have already committed to the land, so we need this." That transfers your problem to them and tells them you have no alternative.
  • "Council will support us anyway." Never imply you will go around staff.

The question behind the question. When the planner asks, "Have you spoken to the neighbours yet?", the real question is, "Will this turn into a fight that lands on my desk?" Answer the real one: "Not yet. We plan an information session before filing and will send you the summary."

When to stay silent. When the planner starts listing concerns, write, do not rebut. Every concern you argue in the room is one you hear less about. Let them finish, then ask, "Of those, which matter most to you?"

Say that out loud now.

"Of those concerns, which matter most to you?"

Worked example one: turning the meeting into numbers

Hypothetical. The note after the meeting says staff could support 50 to 55 units with underground parking, a 3 metre road dedication, a park contribution and a traffic study. You take that note back to Day 5's calculation. At 10 extra units the rezoning fails at any probability, so the decision is made: you either renegotiate the land to its as-of-right value or you walk. One honest hour across a table saved a year of fees. That is what the meeting is for.

Room two: the community information session

The scene. A church hall, forty residents, folding chairs. Two people near the front are angry before you start. Someone is filming on a phone.

Lines to say:

  • "I am Mr Shabazz. I am considering this site, and I wanted you to hear about it from me before anything is filed."
  • "Here is what the rules allow today, without asking anyone: about 45 units at four storeys." Showing the as-of-right building first changes the debate from "this or nothing" to "this or that."
  • "What worries you most?" Then write the answers on a flip chart where the room can see them.
  • "I do not know the answer to that yet. I will find out and put it on the project page within two weeks."

Lines never to say:

  • "Traffic will not be a problem." You do not know that, and a resident who has sat in that traffic does.
  • "Property values will go up." Some will hear it as a threat about taxes or rents.
  • "We need the density for the numbers to work." Your margin is not their concern, and it invites the reply that your numbers are not their problem.

The question behind the question. "How many units?" usually means "Will my street change?" "Who are you?" usually means "Will you still be here if it goes wrong?" Answer with specifics about the street and about how to reach you.

Worked example two: handling the angry front row

A resident stands: "You people just want to cram in as many units as you can and leave." Do not defend your motives. Acknowledge, bridge, answer. "I hear that you have seen projects like that. Here is what is actually proposed, and here is what we would commit to in writing: construction hours, a contact number answered by a person, and a parking count above the minimum." Then stop talking. Silence after a specific answer is stronger than a second paragraph.

Holding your state

A hostile room speeds your breathing and your speech. Before you stand, while you are still seated, take three slow breaths with a long exhale; this is a practitioner habit, and check any breathing practice with your doctor. Speak at half your normal pace. Keep your hands visible and still. If you feel heat rising, look at the flip chart, read the concern aloud, and answer it. Reading slows you down and shows you listened.

Ethics thread: the cleanest file in the room

Planning is where the pressure to bend rules is greatest, because one decision can be worth more than a year of construction profit. Many systems restrict gifts to officials, require lobbying to be registered, and treat any benefit offered to influence a decision as a serious offence. Offer nothing of value to staff or elected members. Not lunch, not tickets, not help for a relative. If anyone suggests an approval can be speeded up for a fee outside the published schedule, end the conversation, write down what was said, and take legal advice. Verify the rules where you build.

The deeper reason is commercial as well as moral. An approval obtained improperly can be challenged and quashed, a lender will not fund on it, and a buyer will not pay for it. Your reputation with planners is an asset you carry from site to site, and it is worth more than any single approval.

The biggest risk

Overpromising to calm a room. A promise made in a hall becomes the expectation in every later meeting, and if you break it you lose the room for good. The control: promise only what you can put in writing, and put it in writing within the time you said.

The beginner's mistake

Bringing a polished rendering to the first meeting. It says the design is finished and the consultation is theatre. Bring a massing sketch and a set of questions.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught "I'll confirm by Friday": the discipline of not answering what you do not know, and following up on time. It is the most valuable line in both rooms this week. A community that sees you return with an answer when you said you would starts to believe the rest of what you say.

Recap

In the planner's room, listen first, ask what would make the scheme supportable, and get the advice in writing before you waive anything. In the hall, show the as-of-right building, ask what worries people, answer specifically and follow up on time. Offer nothing of value to anyone deciding your application. Next: Kema closes the week, with Cole in the Auditor's Chair.
checklist: Hold the pre-application meeting before waiving purchase conditions
Ask staff what would make the scheme supportable and what would make it hard
Write down concerns without rebutting them in the room
Ask for a short written note confirming the advice
Show the community the as-of-right building first
Promise only what you will put in writing, and follow up on time
Offer nothing of value to any official or elected member
Record and report any improper suggestion and take legal advice
head: Field checklist
speak: Two rooms decide most entitlements. In the planner's office, go before you waive your purchase conditions. Say you want their concerns before you design further. Ask what would make your scheme supportable and what would make it hard, which studies they expect, and what conditions are typical. When they list concerns, write, do not argue, then ask which matter most. Get the advice confirmed in a short note and run it through your numbers. In the community hall, introduce yourself, show the as-of-right building first, ask what worries people and write it where they can see it. Never say traffic will not be a problem, and never tell them you need the density for your numbers. Acknowledge, bridge, answer, then stop. Promise only what you will put in writing. And offer nothing of value to anyone who decides your application.
terms: Pre-application consultation — an informal meeting with planning staff before an application is filed, to learn their likely position and requirements.
Community information session — a public meeting where a developer presents a proposal and hears residents' concerns before or during an application.
Lobbying registration — a requirement in some systems that people who seek to influence public officials register and disclose that activity.

hostile.q: A council member's assistant says the application could move faster if you made a donation to a local charity the member supports. What do you do?
hostile.a: I decline, I end the conversation politely, I write down exactly what was said with the date and time, and I take legal advice that day. An approval tied to a benefit can be quashed, and no lender or buyer will rely on it. The application moves at the published pace, through staff.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Entitlements week review, with Cole in the Auditor's Chair
summary: Six questions on the zoning envelope, the price of a permission, conditions and appeals, then a recap of the week. Cole reads a hypothetical entitlement memo as a hostile auditor would, and the boardroom drill asks you to explain entitlement risk in two minutes.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week comes down to one sentence: price land on what the rules allow today, and pay for anything more only when it has been granted and can no longer be taken away. Today you prove you can say it, calculate it and defend it.

Recall

Q. What are the four parts of a risk-adjusted entitlement value?

A. The uplift, multiplied by the probability of approval, minus the expected cost of conditions, minus pursuit costs and the carrying cost of time.

Q. Why should a buyer read the condominium declaration before buying a unit or a site within a condominium?

A. Because it sets the rules, the shared elements, the cost-sharing and the restrictions every owner is bound by, and it can limit what you may do with the property.

Q. Who decides whether a tax arrangement is avoidance or evasion in a dispute?

A. Ultimately the tax authority and then the courts, applying the law and the facts. Your adviser's opinion is evidence of care, not a guarantee. Verify the position against the primary source.

Why this matters

Entitlement knowledge is tested when someone is pushing: a seller who wants the full price, a broker with a deadline, a planner listing conditions, a lender asking why your land value assumes density you do not have. Answering from memory, out loud, is the practice that holds under that pressure. Answer each question before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the six dimensions of a zoning envelope and the rule for finding the building.

Answer: Use, density, height, setbacks, coverage and parking. Compute each limit separately; the smallest one is your building.

Question 2. What makes a building as-of-right, and why does it matter for land price?

Answer: It complies fully with current zoning and needs only a building permit, not a discretionary decision. The as-of-right building is the only one the land price should assume, because it is the only one you own.

Question 3. In Day 5's example, why could a 10-unit rezoning never pay?

Answer: Its fixed costs of pursuit and carry, about 353,000 dollars, exceeded the 320,000 dollars it would win after conditions even if approval were certain. The break-even probability came out above 100 percent.

Question 4. What two ideas, taught through two United States Supreme Court cases, limit what an authority may demand as a condition?

Answer: An essential nexus between the condition and the project's impact, and rough proportionality between them. Verify how the principle applies where you build.

Question 5. Three questions decide how much timeline risk an appeal carries. Name them.

Answer: Who has standing to appeal, what the deadline is, and whether the appeal body hears the matter fresh or only reviews the original decision.

Question 6. What was Rule 32?

Answer: I pay today only for the zoning a site has today; any price for density not yet granted is paid only when the approval is final and free of appeal.

Say that out loud now.

Say Rule 32 without looking, then the four parts of an entitlement's value.

Recap of the week

Day 1, Pax: the envelope, as-of-right versus discretionary, and the ladder of approvals. Day 2, Ford with Cole: a composite developer who paid for a rezoning before it was granted. Day 3, Sage: uplift times probability, minus conditions, pursuit and time, and pursuit money as risk capital. Day 4, REGA: policy and rules, conditions that must connect and bear proportion, variances, appeals and development agreements. Day 5, Sage: working backward to the break-even number of extra units and the rational land price. Day 6, Pax: the planner's room and the community hall, and why nothing of value goes to anyone who decides.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Cole reads documents assuming they are wrong until the evidence proves otherwise. Read this hypothetical memo the way a hostile auditor or a lender's credit officer would, and list what you would challenge before reading on.

Entitlement memo, Site B, hypothetical. Zoning: four storeys, floor area ratio 2.0, so 45 units. Target: 70 units, consistent with the precedent approval on the next block. Probability of approval: high. Land price: 3,500,000 dollars, all due on closing, justified by the appraisal at 70 units. Conditions: expected to be minor. Pursuit budget: 80,000 dollars. Timeline: council approval month 9, construction start month 10. Pre-application meeting: to be booked after closing. Recommendation: waive conditions this week.

The challenges, revealed:

  1. Units from density alone. No setback, coverage or parking check, so 45 units is unproven. Ask for the binding limit.
  2. A precedent treated as a promise. Ask for the differences between the two sites: frontage, servicing, opposition, policy at the time.
  3. "High" is not a probability. Ask for a number, its reasons, and the planner's independent figure.
  4. Price all due on closing at target density. Rule 32 broken. Ask for the as-of-right value and a step-up tied to final approval.
  5. The appraisal's instruction. An appraisal told to assume 70 units proves nothing about 70 units. Ask for the instruction letter.
  6. Conditions "minor" with no estimate. Ask for a schedule with costs and a cost consultant's sign-off.
  7. Construction one month after council. No appeal period, no development agreement, no building permit time. Ask for the approvals register.
  8. Pre-application after closing. The cheapest information arrives after the money has gone.
  9. Pursuit budget of 80,000 dollars for a 70-unit rezoning. Likely too low, and nowhere is it sized against the developer's liquidity.

An auditor's last question is always the same: what in this file was written before the decision, and what was written to justify it? Here, almost nothing predates the price.

Boardroom drill

Set a two-minute timer and explain entitlement risk to an imaginary investment committee. Then compare with the model.

Model answer: "Every site has a zoning envelope: the building the current rules allow. We compute each limit, use, density, height, setbacks, coverage and parking, and the smallest one is the building we own. We price the land on that as-of-right scheme. Anything more is a request, and we value it as the uplift times our documented probability of approval, minus conditions, pursuit costs and the carry while we wait. Small rezonings often fail that test at any probability. Where one passes, we pay the seller for the extra density only when the approval is final and the appeal period has run. We meet planning staff before we waive conditions, we get their advice in writing, we consult the community before filing, and nothing of value goes to anyone who decides. Our approvals register tracks each item from granted to final to security released."

Score yourself

Score your attempt from 1 to 5 on each of four tests. Accuracy: were the numbers and terms correct, with nothing invented? Structure: bottom line first, then method, then controls? Composure: did you pause rather than fill silence? The hard question: did you say what happens when the seller refuses a step-up, which is that you walk? Reread only the lesson behind your lowest score, then answer the hostile question below aloud before reading the model.

The biggest risk

Knowing Rule 32 and breaking it under competitive pressure. The control is the Auditor's Chair turned on yourself: before you waive any condition, list which documents in your file predate the price.

The beginner's mistake

Reviewing by rereading. It feels like work and builds false confidence. Close the lesson and answer aloud; the struggle to recall is what makes it stay.

Callback

In Week 28 you learned to write the go or no-go decision before you are emotionally invested in a site. Entitlement is where that discipline is tested hardest, because the uplift is visible and exciting. The written as-of-right valuation is your go or no-go, made before the excitement.

Recap

The envelope sets what you own; the entitlement calculation sets what more is worth; the law limits what can be demanded of you; the contract decides who carries the risk until approval is final. head: The six questions
speak: Entitlements come down to one rule: price land on what the rules allow today, and pay for anything more only when it has been granted and can no longer be taken away. The envelope has six dimensions, use, density, height, setbacks, coverage and parking, and the smallest limit is your building. That as-of-right scheme sets the land price. An extra approval is worth the uplift times a documented probability, minus conditions, pursuit costs and the carry. Small rezonings often fail at any probability. Conditions are normal, but they should connect to your project and bear some proportion to it. Appeals turn on standing, deadline and how the appeal is heard. In the Auditor's Chair, the question is always which documents were written before the price, and which were written to justify it.
terms: Approvals register — a list tracking each approval from granted to final, conditions met, agreement signed and security released.
Appraisal instruction — the assumptions a client gives an appraiser, which shape and limit what the valuation proves.
Auditor's Chair — reading a document as a hostile reviewer would, assuming each claim is unproven until evidenced.

hostile.q: Your competitor closed on a similar site unconditionally at the full price and got the rezoning. Aren't you just too cautious to win land?
hostile.a: One competitor's outcome is a single result, not a reference class. I will lose some sites to buyers who carry risk I will not. Over a career, the sites I win at as-of-right value with a step-up for approval are the ones that cannot sink me when an approval shrinks or stalls. Caution here is the price of staying in the business long enough to compound.
